# Balanced Brackets — Explained, One Approach at a Time

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-explained.mjs from src/data/problems/stack/balanced-brackets.ts.
     Edit the data, then run `npm run docs:explained`. Edits here are overwritten. -->

**Stack** · easy · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/valid-parentheses/)

Given a string of the characters ()[]{} only, decide whether it is well-formed: every opener has a matching closer of the same kind, closed in last-opened-first-closed order.

## What the input promises

- 1 <= s.length <= 10^4
- s holds only the six characters ()[]{}
- every closer must match the most recent unclosed opener

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `s = "([{}])"` | `true` | — |
| `s = "(]"` | `false` | — |
| `s = "("` | `false` | Unclosed opener left over. |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. "Last opened, first closed" is the literal definition of a stack.
2. Push openers. On a closer, the top of the stack must be its partner.
3. Two failure modes: mismatch mid-string, and a non-empty stack at the end.

</details>

---

## 1. Repeated replace

Keep deleting adjacent matched pairs ("()", "[]", "{}") until nothing changes; valid iff empty. Cute one-liner logic, quadratic runtime — good to know why it's worse, not to use.

```python
def is_balanced(s: str) -> bool:
    prev = None
    while prev != s:
        prev = s
        s = s.replace("()", "").replace("[]", "").replace("{}", "")
    return s == ""
```

**O(n²) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public boolean isBalanced(String s) {
    String prev;
    do {
        prev = s;
        s = s.replace("()", "").replace("[]", "").replace("{}", "");
    } while (!prev.equals(s));
    return s.isEmpty();
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
bool isBalanced(const string& input) {
    string s = input;
    string prev;
    do {
        prev = s;
        size_t pos;
        while ((pos = s.find("()")) != string::npos) s.erase(pos, 2);
        while ((pos = s.find("[]")) != string::npos) s.erase(pos, 2);
        while ((pos = s.find("{}")) != string::npos) s.erase(pos, 2);
    } while (prev != s);
    return s.empty();
}
```

</details>

## 2. The one to remember

> **Why now.** Deleting matched pairs rescans the whole string after every deletion. A stack remembers what is still open as you go, so one pass decides it.

Scan once. Push each opening bracket. For each closing bracket, the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the corresponding opener — otherwise the string is invalid. After the scan the stack must be empty, or some opener was never closed.

```python
def is_balanced(s: str) -> bool:
    partner = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    st: list[str] = []
    for ch in s:
        if ch in partner:
            if not st or st.pop() != partner[ch]:
                return False
        else:
            st.append(ch)
    return not st
```

**O(n) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public boolean isBalanced(String s) {
    Map<Character, Character> partner = new HashMap<>();
    partner.put(')', '(');
    partner.put(']', '[');
    partner.put('}', '{');
    List<Character> st = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
        char ch = s.charAt(i);
        if (partner.containsKey(ch)) {
            if (st.isEmpty() || st.remove(st.size()-1) != partner.get(ch))
                return false;
        } else {
            st.add(ch);
        }
    }
    return st.isEmpty();
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
bool isBalanced(const string& s) {
    unordered_map<char, char> partner{{')','('},{']','['},{'}','{'}};
    vector<char> st;
    for (char ch : s) {
        auto it = partner.find(ch);
        if (it != partner.end()) {
            if (st.empty() || st.back() != it->second) return false;
            st.pop_back();
        } else {
            st.push_back(ch);
        }
    }
    return st.empty();
}
```

</details>

| 2 | The one to remember | O(n) time · O(n) space | Deleting matched pairs rescans the whole string after every deletion. A stack remembers what is still open as you go, so one pass decides it. |

## Full runnable script

Every rung in one file, printed against the inputs `npm run verify:run`
drives the Java and C++ blocks with. Run it: `python explained.py`.

```python
def is_balanced_repeated_replace(s: str) -> bool:
    prev = None
    while prev != s:
        prev = s
        s = s.replace("()", "").replace("[]", "").replace("{}", "")
    return s == ""


def is_balanced_the_one_to_remember(s: str) -> bool:
    partner = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    st: list[str] = []
    for ch in s:
        if ch in partner:
            if not st or st.pop() != partner[ch]:
                return False
        else:
            st.append(ch)
    return not st

APPROACHES = [
    is_balanced_repeated_replace,
    is_balanced_the_one_to_remember,
]

# the same inputs npm run verify:run drives the Java and C++ blocks with:
# a mismatch of the right shape but wrong kind, and a close with nothing open — '(]', ']'
CASES = [
    lambda: ("()",),
    lambda: ("()[]{}",),
    lambda: ("(]",),
    lambda: ("([)]",),
    lambda: ("{[]}",),
    lambda: ("]",),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for fn in APPROACHES:
        answers = []
        for make in CASES:
            try:
                answers.append(fn(*make()))
            except BaseException as exc:  # a rung that raises names itself
                answers.append(f"!{exc}")
        print(f"{fn.__name__:<33} -> {answers}")
```
